clinicalPearls: Caused by Basidiobolus ranarum, an environmental fungus of the order Entomophthorales found in soil, decaying vegetation, and the gut of amphibians, reptiles, and insects
Unlike angioinvasive mucormycosis, it typically affects immunocompetent hosts and follows a chronic, indolent course
The classic form is subcutaneous, producing a firm, painless, slowly enlarging plaque on the trunk or limbs, most often in children in tropical regions
An increasingly recognised gastrointestinal form presents with abdominal pain, a palpable mass, and eosinophilia, frequently mimicking Crohn's disease or an abdominal malignancy
Histology shows broad, thin-walled, sparsely septate hyphae surrounded by eosinophilic material in the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, with a marked eosinophilic infiltrate
Diagnosis is often made only after surgical resection, as pre-operative imaging and endoscopy suggest tumour or inflammatory bowel disease
Treatment combines prolonged antifungal therapy, typically with itraconazole or another azole, and surgical excision or debulking where feasible
reference.pathophysiology: Basidiobolus ranarum is a saprophytic mould of the Entomophthorales that lives in soil and decaying plant matter and colonises the gastrointestinal tracts of amphibians, reptiles, and insects. Human subcutaneous disease is thought to follow inoculation through minor skin trauma or insect bites, while gastrointestinal disease probably results from ingestion of contaminated soil, food, or water. In the tissues the fungus provokes a chronic granulomatous and intensely eosinophilic inflammatory response rather than the vascular invasion typical of true zygomycetes, so infarction is uncommon. The hyphae are surrounded by eosinophilic Splendore-Hoeppli material, and the reaction slowly forms fibrotic masses. In the bowel this transmural inflammation and mass effect closely imitates Crohn's disease or carcinoma, and can lead to obstruction or perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Crohn's disease and other inflammatory bowel disease
Mucormycosis and other invasive mould infections
Soft-tissue sarcoma or other subcutaneous tumours
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy with histopathology showing broad sparsely septate hyphae and the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon
Fungal culture of tissue to identify Basidiobolus
Full blood count demonstrating peripheral eosinophilia
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) to define the extent of a mass and organ involvement
Endoscopy with biopsy in gastrointestinal disease
Molecular identification by PCR and sequencing where culture is unrevealing
redFlags: Bowel obstruction or perforation from a gastrointestinal mass
Rapid enlargement or systemic spread of disease
Extensive organ involvement (liver, colon) on imaging
Diagnostic confusion leading to inappropriate cancer or Crohn's therapy
reference.prognosis: Subcutaneous disease usually responds well to prolonged antifungal therapy with a good outlook; gastrointestinal disease carries higher morbidity because of late diagnosis and complications, though combined surgery and antifungals achieve cure in many patients.
pitfalls: Mistaking gastrointestinal disease for Crohn's disease or malignancy and giving immunosuppression or oncological treatment
Stopping antifungal therapy prematurely, allowing relapse of this indolent infection
Confusing it with angioinvasive mucormycosis and expecting a fulminant course
Overlooking the diagnostic clue of marked eosinophilia with a chronic mass
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give prolonged systemic antifungal therapy with an oral azole, itraconazole being first-line, continued for months until clinical and radiological resolution
Use saturated potassium iodide as an adjunct or alternative for subcutaneous disease where azoles are unavailable or poorly tolerated
Consider alternative azoles such as voriconazole or posaconazole for refractory or extensive gastrointestinal disease
Combine surgical resection or debridement of localised gastrointestinal masses with antifungal therapy, as diagnosis is often made at operation
Monitor peripheral eosinophilia, inflammatory markers and serial imaging to gauge response and guide treatment duration
Avoid unnecessary immunosuppression and treat coexisting infection or malnutrition supportively
Refer to infectious diseases and surgical teams for combined medical-surgical management
